One shorthand you will see everywhere, and which this book uses from the next lesson onward: since C99 you can declare the counter right in the first slot — for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++). The variable then exists only inside the loop, which is usually what you want: it cannot collide with anything outside, and it disappears when the loop ends. Declaring i above the loop still works, and is what you need when you want to read the counter after the loop finishes.

Cpp_Book_Lesson_2_7.html
Pointers have two things that could be constant: the value they point at, and the pointer itself.

A one-paragraph pointer primer, since pointers get their own lesson at 2.9: a pointer is a variable that stores another variable's address instead of a value of its own. int* p = &x; makes p hold the address of x. Writing *p means "the thing living at that address", so *p = 7; puts 7 into x, while p = &y; re-aims p at a different variable entirely. Two separate things, then — the address in the pointer, and the value at that address — which is exactly why const gets interesting here.

if (auto it = myMap.find(key); it != myMap.end()) {
    use(it->second);       // 'it' is in scope here
} else {
    std::cout << "not found\n";  // and here too
}
// 'it' is gone — out of scope, can't be misused

if (auto at = email.find('@'); at != std::string::npos) {
    use(at);               // 'at' is in scope here
} else {
    std::cout << "not an address\n";  // and here too
}
// 'at' is gone — out of scope, can't be misused
